# Conversion Constructors
<!-- Slide 19 -->

## Going the Other Way? {.smaller}

- `Temperature today = 21.5;` already compiles. Why?

::: notes
Slides 20–27


:::

<!-- Slide 20 -->

---

## How Many Constructor Calls?

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}
~~~cpp
class Temperature {
private:
    double celsius;

public:
    Temperature(double value = 0.0) {
        celsius = value;
        cout << "Temperature(" << value << ")" << endl;
    }
};

int main() {
    Temperature today = 21.5;
    cout << "done" << endl;
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::

. . .

Output: `Temperature(21.5)` then `done`

::: notes
main never names the constructor, yet it runs once. Let students commit to a number before revealing.

Full program: cpp/constructor_count.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 21 -->

---

## You Already Wrote One

- 07.02's constructor: `Temperature(double value = 0.0)`
- It can be called with one `double`, so the compiler may use it to turn a `double` into a `Temperature`.
- A constructor that is not `explicit` and can take a single value is a converting constructor.

::: notes
Reading: textbook section 11.10, Convert Constructors; learncpp 14.16, Converting constructors and the explicit keyword.
:::

<!-- Slide 22 -->

---

## Which Constructors Convert from One Value?

| Constructor | Converts a single value? |
|---|---|
| `Temperature()` | No: takes nothing |
| `Temperature(double c)` | Yes: `double` to `Temperature` |
| `Temperature(double c = 0.0)` | Yes: the default does not matter |
| `Temperature(double c, char unit)` | No: needs two values |
| `Temperature(double c, char unit = 'C')` | Yes: the second parameter has a default |

::: notes
Since C++11 any constructor that is not explicit also takes part in brace initialization, so Temperature t = {21.5, 'F'}; uses the two-argument constructor. The table covers conversion from one value, which is the case that happens silently.
:::

<!-- Slide 23 -->

---

## What the Compiler Builds

- `Temperature today = 21.5;` asks for a `Temperature` built from `21.5`.
- The compiler calls `Temperature(double)` to build it.
- No constructor call appears in the source code.

::: notes
Formally the rule builds a temporary Temperature and initializes today from it. Since C++17 that copy is guaranteed to be skipped, which is why the program printed one constructor call, not two.
:::

<!-- Slide 24 -->

---

## You Use This Every Day

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}
~~~cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

void greet(const string& name);

int main() {
    string course = "CISP 400";   // C-string to string
    greet("Ada");                 // the same conversion, in a call
    cout << course << endl;
    return 0;
}

void greet(const string& name) {
    cout << "Hello, " << name << endl;
}
~~~
:::

::: notes
string has a converting constructor from a C-string. That conversion is why a string literal works anywhere a string is expected. Here the conversion is convenient on purpose.

Full program: cpp/string_conversion.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 25 -->

---

## Two Directions, One Class

| Direction | Written as | Lives in |
|---|---|---|
| `Temperature` to `double` | `operator double() const` | `Temperature` |
| `double` to `Temperature` | `Temperature(double)` | `Temperature` |

- Add an `operator+` and `today + 5.0` has two possible routes. Topic 5 shows what the compiler does with them.

::: notes

:::

<!-- Slide 26 -->

---

## Summary

- A constructor that can take one value converts that value's type into the class.
- The conversion is convenient when you intend it, as with `string`, and a surprise when you do not.

::: notes

:::
